newsitem.title: USA: Boeing may relax exclusive supply pacts.
newsitem.headline: Boeing may relax exclusive supply pacts.

text.p: Boeing Co. may be willing to relax terms of its exclusive deals to supply aircraft to three major airlines to placate concerns in Europe about its proposed merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp.

According to a report Wednesday in the Wall Street Journal, the world's largest aircraft manufacturer may drop exclusivity provisions in its supply contracts with American Airlines, Continental Airlines Inc. and Delta Air Lines Inc. to ensure that European Union regulators will approve the $14 billion merger, which was announced in December.

Officials from Boeing declined to comment on the report but said the company was confident the merger will be approved by the Federal Trade Commission as soon as July 1, and by the EU's executive Commission shortly after.
"We remain confident that both the FTC and the EC reviews will have positive outcomes," Boeing spokeswoman Sherry Nebelsaid. "We feel confident that there will be a positive outcome."
An executive at one U.S. airline, which has signed an exclusive aircraft supply pact with Boeing, said it would favour the removal of the exclusivity clause from its contract.

"It would be in our favour because we got a good price on the jets and now we might not be wedded to the exclusivity clause," he said. "You have still got to live with (Boeing), and do business with them. If you don't do it in written language, will they do it with a nod and a wink?"

The European concerns stem from the three exclusive supply pacts Boeing recently signed for firm orders for over $16 billion. The 20-year exclusive deals were even more lucrative with options included. The American Airlines deal alone was said to be worth in the region of $20 billion if all the options were excercised.
European leaders have said the exclusive pacts were an obstacle to the approval of the merger because they make it difficult for European aircraft maker Airbus Industrie to compete.

EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has made it clear the Boeing/McDonnell Douglas merger will not be approved as it stands and has said the exclusive pacts were not the Commission's only concern.

Under EU law, the Commission must probe all mergers involving companies with worldwide revenues of about $6.6 billion and EU sales of about $280 million each, irrespective of their nationality. The 1990 merger law allows the Commission to block a merger completely if the concessions it requires to ensure fair competition are not met.
Analysts said if Boeing were to drop the exclusivity portion of the deals, the merger would likely be approved by the Europeans.

"Obviously they want to get the deal done and that's the major sticking point with the EU," said Cai Von Rumohr, an analyst at Cowen and Co. "This is a concession that would seem logical to make ... there may be other things, or other assurances, but I think this is probably the big one."
But analysts said objections to the exclusive supply pacts may be just smoke and mirrors to disguise an even bigger concession Airbus Industrie had hoped to win.

Paul Nisbet at JSA Research Inc. said Airbus is hoping to reopen the 1992 General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade because it finds its terms too restrictive. Under GATT, governments are restricted in the amount they can give companies for development of new aircraft. That restriction will make it hard for Airbus to get the billions of dollars it needs to develop and produce its proposed A3XX aircraft, Nisbet said.

Airbus, which has about one-third of the commercial aircraft market, compared with Boeing's two-thirds, is considering developing the A3XX to compete with Boeing's popular 747 series. The intercontinental,long-range plane would seat up to 600 people but could cost $10 billion to $15 billion to develop and produce, Nisbet said.
